passages.happening:
‘When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son’ (verse 1). But the more God called, the farther they went from him. They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images (verse 2).

‘It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them in My arms, but they never realized that it was I who healed them’ (verse 3). ‘I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love; I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is spoken almost wholly in God's own voice, and it moves like a parent's anguished speech. The marriage picture of the first chapters gives way to a father and a young child. The exodus from Egypt was the moment God called Israel his son, and the wilderness years and the settling of the land followed, and with them Israel's pull toward the Baals.

Hosea draws on the ordinary life of a household. A parent taught a toddler to walk, carried the child in their arms and fed them by hand. Verse 4 turns to the care of working animals: a good farmer led an ox with cords, eased the yoke from its jaw and bent down to give it food. Both pictures show a God who stoops to his people, patient and tender. The child never realized who was holding him.
passages.later: At the exodus the LORD told Pharaoh, ‘Israel is My firstborn son’ (Exodus 4:22). Matthew tells how the child Jesus was brought back from Egypt, and says this fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet, quoting verse 1: “Out of Egypt I called My Son” (Matthew 2:15).
passages.hard:
How can Matthew say that a verse about the exodus was fulfilled in Jesus?

Read on its own, verse 1 remembers a past event, the exodus. It is not framed as a prediction, and some readers have concluded that Matthew misused it. The main answers turn on what Matthew means by fulfilled. Many interpreters call his reading typological: the patterns of Israel's history, sonship, exile and rescue, find their fullest expression in Jesus, who is the Son in a unique sense and lives Israel's story faithfully. Others point out that Hosea himself goes on to promise a new exodus from Egypt and Assyria (verses 10-11), so the prophet already expected God's past act to be repeated in a greater way.

On either view, Matthew is not claiming that Hosea foresaw Jesus' childhood. He is claiming that Jesus' life completes the story Hosea was telling.
passages.asks: God taught Ephraim to walk, and Ephraim never realized who was holding him. Ask where God may have carried you without your knowing it. And ask what it means to you that God describes his love in the plain tasks of a parent.

passages.t: Back to Egypt, ruled by Assyria
passages.happening: ‘Will they not return to the land of Egypt and be ruled by Assyria because they refused to repent?’ (verse 5). A sword will flash through their cities and break the bars of their gates, and their own plans will devour them (verse 6). God's people are set on turning from him. They call to the Most High, but he will not lift them up (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The threat in the present is Assyria, which under Tiglath-pileser III, who reigned from 745 to 727 BC, and the kings after him was pushing west and making Israel a vassal. Verse 5 joins two pictures. Israel will go back to Egypt, the symbol of the slavery it was rescued from, and it will be ruled by Assyria. Some Israelites may well have fled to Egypt, and Hoshea, Israel's last king, sought Egyptian help against Assyria, but the main fulfillment came with Assyria's conquest of Samaria.

The word for turn runs through these verses. Israel will not return to God, so God will return Israel to a new Egypt. The son who was called out of Egypt is going back.
passages.later: Hoshea sent to So king of Egypt and stopped paying tribute, and the king of Assyria came against Samaria (2 Kings 17:4-6). The law had warned that the LORD would send a disobedient people back to Egypt (Deuteronomy 28:68).
passages.asks: The son called out of slavery was heading back into it. Ask whether there is something God freed you from that you keep returning to. And ask what it would take for you to turn back to him instead.

passages.t: A heart turned over, and a call home
passages.happening:
Then God's heart breaks open. ‘How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel? How could I make you like Admah? How could I treat you like Zeboiim?’ (verse 8). His heart is turned within him, and his compassion is stirred.

‘I will not execute the full fury of My anger; I will not turn back to destroy Ephraim’ (verse 9). He is God and not a man, the Holy One among them, and he will not come in wrath. They will follow the LORD, and he will roar like a lion. When he roars, his children will come trembling from the west, from Egypt like birds and from Assyria like doves, and he will settle them in their homes (verses 10-11).

Ephraim surrounds God with lies, Israel with deceit, but Judah still walks with God (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Admah and Zeboiim were cities of the plain destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah. Hosea's hearers knew them as bywords for total ruin. For God to ask how he could make Israel like them is to say that the full sentence Israel deserves is one he cannot bring himself to carry out.

The Hebrew of verse 8 says God's heart has turned over within him, the same verb used for the overthrow of Sodom and its sister cities. The overturning happens inside God, not to Israel. And the reason is striking. In verse 9 God's holiness is the reason he will not destroy them: he is not like a human being whose anger runs its course to the end.

The lion's roar in verse 10 is not the roar of an attacker. It is a call home, and the children come trembling, like birds flying back. Verse 12 begins a new section in the Hebrew text, where it is numbered 12:1, and leads into the charges of chapter 12.
passages.later: Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23). Isaiah heard the same promise of a second gathering: the Lord will reach out his hand ‘a second time to recover the remnant of His people’ (Isaiah 11:11).
passages.asks: God asks how he could give up the people who had left him. Ask what it means to you that God's holiness is the reason for his mercy here, not the limit of it. And ask whether you have believed that God could give you up.
